Paragraph:
Translation: In charge of the various necessities of life, the demigods, being satisfied by the performance of yajna [sacrifice], supply all necessities to man. But he who enjoys these gifts, without offering them to the demigods in return, is certainly a thief.

Purport (Excerpt): ...all the necessities of life that the human society requires are supplied by the demigod agents of the Lord. No one can manufacture anything... If we forget the purpose of human life and simply take supplies from the agents of the Lord for sense gratification... certainly we become thieves, and therefore we are punished by the laws of material nature. A society of thieves can never be happy...
Situation/Problem_Faced: Entitlement and ungrateful consumption of natural and societal gifts without offering gratitude or contribution.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna labels those who consume life's gifts without offering back in sacrifice as thieves (stena eva sah). Gratitude and contribution are essential moral obligations.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna is shown that taking without giving breeds societal instability and personal guilt.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Gratitude vs. Entitlement: Replacing the belief of being owed with active appreciation for supplied gifts
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Social Responsibility: Acknowledging one's debt to the natural world and society
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Ethical Consumption: Using resources mindfully and returning value to the ecosystem

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Stena (A thief; one who consumes without giving back or offering gratitude)
Ishta-bhogan (The desired necessities of life provided by cosmic order)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The necessities of life are gifts provided by divine order. Anyone who consumes these resources for personal gratification without offering gratitude or sacrifice in return acts as a thief, incurring karmic reactions and losing spiritual peace.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Entitlement—expecting benefits without contributing—creates underlying feelings of guilt, alienation, and chronic dissatisfaction. Practicing gratitude and acknowledging our dependence on wider systems fosters humility, grounding, and genuine psychological contentment.
